verses.zh: 到那日，耶和华必用他刚硬有力的大刀刑罚鳄鱼―就是那快行的蛇，刑罚鳄鱼―就是那曲行的蛇，并杀海中的大鱼。
verses.en: At that time[NOTE:1] the Lord will punishwith his destructive,[NOTE:2] great, and powerful swordLeviathan the fast-moving[NOTE:3] serpent,Leviathan the squirming serpent;he will kill the sea monster.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “in that day” (so KJV).
Heb “hard, severe”; cf. NAB, NRSV “cruel”; KJV “sore”; NLT “terrible.”
Heb “fleeing” (so NAB, NASB, NRSV). Some translate “slippery” or “slithering.” See the same Hebrew phrase in Job 26:13.

The description of Leviathan should be compared with the following excerpts from Ugaritic mythological texts: (1) “Was not the dragon (Ugaritic tnn, cognate with Hebrew תַנִּין [tannin, translated “sea monster” here]) vanquished and captured? I did destroy the wriggling (Ugaritic ʿqltn, cognate to Hebrew עֲקַלָּתוֹן [ʿaqallaton, translated “squirming” here]) serpent, the tyrant with seven heads (cf. Ps 74:14).” (See CTA 3 iii 38-39.) (2) “for all that you smote Leviathan the slippery (Ugaritic brh, cognate to Hebrew בָּרִחַ [bariakh, translated “fast-moving” here]) serpent, [and] made an end of the wriggling serpent, the tyrant with seven heads” (See CTA 5 i 1-3.) sn In the Ugaritic mythological texts Leviathan is a sea creature that symbolizes the destructive water of the sea and in turn the forces of chaos that threaten the established order. Isaiah here applies imagery from Canaanite mythology to Yahweh’s eschatological victory over his enemies. Elsewhere in the OT, the battle with the sea motif is applied to Yahweh’s victories over the forces of chaos at creation and in history (cf. Pss 74:13-14; 77:16-20; 89:9-10; Isa 51:9-10). Yahweh’s subjugation of the chaos waters is related to His kingship (cf. Pss 29:3, 10; 93:3-4). Apocalyptic literature employs the imagery as well. The beasts of Dan 7 emerge from the sea, while Rev 13 speaks of a seven-headed beast coming from the sea.
verses.commentary:
27:1 "In that day" See note at Isa. 2:11.

▣ "Leviathan the fleeing serpent" Leviathan (BDB 531) seems to be a Ugaritic mythological sea
animal (i.e. Job 41:19-21) mentioned in Job 3:8; Ps. 104:26; Amos 9:3. However, sometimes it is used as a
symbol for an evil nation (cf. Ps. 74:13-14, possibly Egypt). It resembles a river snaking through their land.
Sometimes this term is linked specifically to "Rahab," which is a way of referring to Egypt (cf. Ps. 87:4;
89:9-10; and Isa. 30:7). It seems to me that, in context, we are talking about a river symbolizing a national
enemy, either Egypt or Assyria (cf. Isa. 27:12). The reason this term can be used symbolically so easily is
that it was previously used in some of the mythological literature of Canaan (cf. Ps. 74:12-17; see
G. Archer, Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties, pp. 239-240).

There is a parallelism between

- the fleeing serpent (BDB 638 I) or sea monster (NASB footnote)

- the twisted sea monster

- the dragon who lives in the sea

This same allusion is found in (1) Ugaritic poems and (2) Isa. 51:9, using "Rahab," who is
also identified by the term "dragon" (BDB 1072). See
SPECIAL TOPIC: LEVIATHAN

The only apparent connection between this verse and the context is Isa. 27:11-12.

- YHWH as creator, Isa. 27:11

- flowing streams of the Euphrates and the brook of Egypt in Isa. 27:12

- the end of time is like the beginning of time (i.e. Genesis 1-2; Revelation 21-22)

Apparently Isaiah is a compilation of his writings over many years and compiled on the basis
of word plays or themes, not chronological history.

▣ "dragon" This term (BDB 1072) means

- serpent, Exod. 7:9,10,12; Deut. 32:33; Ps. 91:13

- dragon, Neh. 2:13; Jer. 51:34

- sea/river monster, Gen. 1:21; Job 7:12; Ps. 74:13; 148:7. It is parallel to Leviathan (cf.
Psalm 74:13-14). It is used as imagery for Egypt in Isa. 27:1; 51:9,10; Ezek. 29:3; 32:2.

SPECIAL TOPIC: A GREAT RED DRAGON

The two great river systems of the Ancient Near East were the cradles of
its civilizations (i.e. the Nile and the Tigris/Euphrates).

Tanin (BDB 1072) is parallel with

- Leviathan, Ps. 74:13-14; Isa. 27:1

- Rahab, Isa. 51:9

- Bashan, Ps. 68:22; Amos 9:3 (cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 87)

The Jewish Publication Society of America (JPSOA) has an interesting footnote to "the Dragon of the Sea."

"The monster which the Lord vanquished of old (cf. 51:9; Ps. 74:13-14) was the embodiment of chaos; here it
stands for the forces of evil in the present world." p. 835 of the Jewish Study Bible.

verses.en: When that time comes,[NOTE:1] sing about a delightful vineyard![NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “in that day” (so KJV).
Heb “vineyard of delight,” or “vineyard of beauty.” Many medieval mss read כֶּרֶם חֶמֶר (kerem khemer, “vineyard of wine”), i.e., “a productive vineyard.”

27:2

The Hebrew word for "pleasant" is חמד
(BDB 326), which is in the Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia, but DSS has the
ר not the ד. These two Hebrew
letters were often confused by copyists. The Hebrew word for "wine" is
חמר (BDB 330). The vowel points are the same
for both words. The UBS Hebrew Text Project, p. 62, gives "pleasant"a "C" rating (considerable doubt).

The vineyard was a symbol of Israel (cf. Isa. 5:1-7; Peshitta), but here, because of the
universal nature of chapters 24-27, it may be the whole earth (cf. Isa. 26:21; JPSOA footnote). The imagery clearly
refers to Eden (see SPECIAL TOPIC: EDEN).

▣ "sing" This is a Piel IMPERATIVE (BDB 777, KB 854). There
are several "songs" mentioned in this literary unit. See note at Isa. 26:1b.

The Jewish Study Bible, p. 835, has an interesting comment on this "song." It asserts that the
judgment song of Isa. 5:1-7 is contrasted with this restoration and forgiveness song of 27:2-6.

verses.en: “I, the Lord, protect it;[NOTE:1] I water it regularly.[NOTE:2] I guard it night and day,so no one can harm it.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “her.” Apparently “vineyard” is the antecedent, though normally this noun is understood as masculine (see Lev 25:3, however).
Or perhaps, “constantly.” Heb “by moments.”
Heb “lest [someone] visit [harm] upon it, night and day I guard it.”
verses.commentary:
27:3 YHWH had a special relationship, a covenant relationship with the descendants of Abraham. They
were uniquely His people. However, Isa. 27:6 shows He also had a universal plan for all the world (cf.
Gen. 3:15; 12:3; Exod. 19:5).

verses.en: I am not angry.I wish I could confront some thorns and briers!Then I would march against them[NOTE:1] for battle;I would set them[NOTE:2] all on fire,
notes: Heb “it.” The feminine singular suffix apparently refers back to the expression “thorns and briers,” understood in a collective sense. For other examples of a cohortative expressing resolve after a hypothetical statement introduced by מִי with נָתָן (mi with natan), see Judg 9:29; Jer 9:1-2; Ps 55:6.
Heb “it.” The feminine singular suffix apparently refers back to the expression “thorns and briers,” understood in a collective sense.
verses.commentary:
27:4-5 There are several COHORTATIVES and JUSSIVES
in these verses.

- I would step on them, BDB 832, KB 979, Qal COHORTATIVE
(VERB found only here in the OT)

- I would burn them, BDB 428, KB 429, Hiphil IMPERFECT used
in a COHORTATIVE sense

in a JUSSIVE sense, twice

Verse 3 describes YHWH's care and protection for Abraham's descendants and of all
humans made in His image and likeness (Gen. 1:26-27).

- Isa. 27:4 describes His willingness to protect and destroy her enemies

- Isa. 27:5 is a call to trust in His care and protection

- Isa. 27:6 is the result of the blessings which will one day fill the earth (the original intention
of God in Genesis 1)

verses.zh: 不然，让它持住我的能力，使它与我和好，愿它与我和好。
verses.en: unless they became my subjects[NOTE:1] and made peace with me;let them make peace with me.”[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “or let him take hold of my refuge.” The subject of the third masculine singular verb form is uncertain. Apparently the symbolic “thorns and briers” are in view, though in v. 4b a feminine singular pronoun was used to refer to them.

The Hebrew text has, “he makes peace with me; peace he makes with me.” Some contend that two alternative readings are preserved here and one should be deleted. The first has the object שָׁלוֹם (shalom, “peace”) preceding the verb עָשָׂה (ʿasah, “make”); the second reverses the order. Another option is to retain both statements, although repetitive, to emphasize the need to make peace with Yahweh.
verses.commentary:
27:5 "Or let him rely on My protection" This shows that human (even for God's enemies, cf. Isa. 27:4)
response is part of God's plan (cf. Isa. 1:16-17,18-20). There is a paradox in the Bible between the
sovereignty of God in history and God's will that humans respond to Him by faith. Isaiah 27:5 is God's
offering of forgiveness and salvation to those Gentiles who trust in Him (cf. Isa. 2:2-4; 42:6; 45:22; 49:6).

SPECIAL TOPIC: ELECTION

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

▣ "Let him make peace with Me" This phrase is doubled, which is characteristic of this section
of Isaiah. See note at Isa. 26:6.

Peace is such a crucial aspect of a faith relationship with God (cf. Isa. 26:12; 32:17;
52:7; 54:10; 55:12; 57:2,19; 60:17; 66:12; Phil. 4:7,9) and His Messiah (cf. Isa. 9:6,7; 53:5;
Rom. 5:1; John 14:27; 16:33; 20:19,21,26). It also involves peace between nations (cf. Isa. 2:4; 39:8),
but there is no peace for the wicked (cf. Isa. 48:22; 57:1; 59:18).

Here the term denotes a peace treaty, initiated by YHWH, but must be accepted and lived
out by the faithful.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PEACE (OT)

verses.zh: 将来雅各要扎根，以色列要发芽开花；他们的果实必充满世界。
verses.en: The time is coming when Jacob will take root;[NOTE:1] Israel will blossom and grow branches.The produce[NOTE:2] will fill the surface of the world.[NOTE:3]
notes: The Hebrew text reads literally, “the coming ones, let Jacob take root.” הַבָּאִים (habbaʾim, “the coming ones”) should probably be emended to יָמִים בָּאִים (yamim baʾim, “days [are] coming”) or בְּיָמִים הַבָּאִים (biyamim habbaʾim, “in the coming days”).
Heb “fruit” (so KJV, NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV, NLT).
This apparently refers to a future population explosion. See 26:18.
verses.commentary:
27:6 "Israel will blossom and sprout;

And they will fill the whole world with fruit" Here again is the imagery of Mount Zion being raised to the highest
of all mountains and all the other topological barriers eliminated so that all the world can flow to Jerusalem to worship
God (cf. Isa. 2:2-4; 24:23; 25:6,7; 27:13; 56:6; 66:23). This faithfulness is the exact opposite of Isa. 26:18. Maybe
part of the fruit is "raised ones" of Isa. 26:19.

▣ "world" See SPECIAL TOPIC: WORLD (several terms), I. E.

verses.zh: 主击打他们，岂像击打那些击打他们的人吗？他们被杀戮，岂像被他们所杀戮的吗？
verses.en: Has the Lord struck down Israel as he did their oppressors?[NOTE:1] Has Israel been killed like their enemies?[NOTE:2]
notes: The Hebrew text reads literally, “Like the striking down of the one striking him down does he strike him down?” The meaning of the text is unclear, but this may be a rhetorical question, suggesting that Israel has not experienced divine judgment to the same degree as her oppressors. In this case “the one striking…down” refers to Israel’s oppressors, while the pronoun “him” refers to Israel. The subject of the final verb (“does he strike…down”) would then be God, while the pronoun “him” would again refer to Israel.

The Hebrew text reads literally, “Or like the killing of his killed ones is he killed?” If one accepts the interpretation of the parallel line outlined in the previous note, then this line too would contain a rhetorical question suggesting that Israel has not experienced destruction to the same degree as its enemies. In this case “his killed ones” refer to the ones who struck Israel down, and Israel would be the subject of the final verb (“is he killed”).
verses.commentary:
27:7 This is a very difficult verse. It states that God's judgment is going to fall on those
nations that He had used to judge His own people. (cf. Isa. 47:6).

Repetition of words and phrases is characteristic of this literary unit (see Isa. 26:6).
Here the NOUN, מכה (BDB 646,
FEMININE, often used of YHWW bringing judgment on His own people, cf. Lev. 26:21;
Deut. 28:61; Jer. 30:12), "to wound," or "to slaughter," is followed by the repeating of a
related NOUN, נכה (BDB 645, KB 697,
Hiphil PARTICIPLE and Hiphil PERFECT). Those who YHWH
used to punish will be punished even more severely than they punished God's people (NET Bible).

verses.zh: 你打发他们去，是相机宜与他们相争；刮东风的日子，就用暴风将他们逐去。
verses.en: When you summon her for divorce, you prosecute her;[NOTE:1] he drives her away[NOTE:2] with his strong wind in the day of the east wind.[NOTE:3]
notes: The Hebrew text reads literally, “in [?], in sending her away, you oppose her.” The meaning of this line is uncertain. The form בְּסַאסְּאָה (besasseʾah) is taken as an infinitive from סַאסְּאָה (sasseʾah) with a prepositional prefix and a third feminine singular suffix. (The MT does not have a mappiq in the final he [ה], however). According to HALOT 738 s.v. סַאסְּאָה the verb is a Palpel form from an otherwise unattested root cognate with an Arabic verb meaning “to gather beasts with a call.” Perhaps it means “to call, summon” here, but this is a very tentative proposal. בְּשַׁלְחָהּ (beshalekhah, “in sending her away”) appears to be a Piel infinitive with a prepositional prefix and a third feminine singular suffix. Since the Piel of שָׁלָח (shalakh) can sometimes mean “divorce” (HALOT 1514-15 s.v.) and the following verb רִיב (riv, “oppose”) can be used in legal contexts, it is possible that divorce proceedings are alluded to here. This may explain why Israel is referred to as feminine in this verse, in contrast to the masculine forms used in vv. 6-7 and 9.
The Hebrew text has no object expressed, but one can understand a third feminine singular pronominal object and place a mappiq in the final he (ה) of the form to indicate the suffix.
The “east wind” here symbolizes violent divine judgment.
verses.commentary:
27:8 "them" The "them" of Isa. 27:8 refers to Israel being divorced (i.e. "contend," BDB 936,
KB 1224, Qal IMPERFECT, cf. Hosea 2:2) by God because she broke the Mosaic
covenant (cf. Isa. 50:1). Therefore, God brought foreign rulers to judge His people (cf. Deut. 28:49-57;
i.e. Assyria, Isa. 10:5, and Babylon, Isaiah 14). However, God will judge them also (cf. Isa. 27:7; 47:6; 49:25).

I have come to believe this theological affirmation of YHWH divorcing His unfaithful wife, Israel,
is the same theology presented in the book of Revelation. The divorce was the Jewish War with Rome (A.D. 66-70),
which culminated with the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple. The last two chapters of Revelation denote
the wedding banquet of His new faithful wife, the church. See my new Partial Preterist commentary on Revelation online (2024).

▣ "by driving them away" The Hebrew VERB (BDB 212, KB 237, Qal
PERFECT) denotes

▣ "east wind" Often this imagery refers to the powers of Mesopotamia (i.e. Isa. 46:11;

So it must be imagery of divine judgment (cf. Exod. 10:13; Ps. 48:7; Jer. 18:17). Sometimes the east wind
is a divine act of blessing (cf. Exod. 14:21; 15:10; Num. 11:31; see NIDOTTE, vol. 3, pp. 871-873).

verses.zh: 所以，雅各的罪孽得赦免，他的罪过得除掉的果效，全在乎此：就是他叫祭坛的石头变为打碎的灰石，以致木偶和日像不再立起。
verses.en: So in this way Jacob’s sin will be forgiven,[NOTE:1] and this is how they will show they are finished sinning:[NOTE:2] They will make all the stones of the altars[NOTE:3] like crushed limestone,and the Asherah poles and the incense altars will no longer stand.[NOTE:4]
notes: Or “be atoned for” (NIV); cf. NRSV “be expiated.”

Heb “and this [is] all the fruit of removing his sin.” The meaning of the statement is not entirely clear, though “removing his sin” certainly parallels “Jacob’s sin will be removed” in the preceding line. If original, “all the fruit” may refer to the result of the decision to remove sin, but the phrase may be a textual variation of an original לְכַפֵּר (lekhapper, “to atone for”), which in turn might be a gloss on הָסִר (hasir, “removing”).
Heb “when he makes the stones of an altar.” The singular “altar” is collective here; pagan altars are in view, as the last line of the verse indicates. See also 17:8.

As interpreted and translated above, this verse says that Israel must totally repudiate its pagan religious practices in order to experience God’s forgiveness and restoration. Another option is to understand “in this way” and “this” in v. 9a as referring back to the judgment described in v. 8. In this case כָּפַר (kafar, “atone for”) is used in a sarcastic sense; Jacob’s sin is “atoned for” and removed through severe judgment. Following this line of interpretation, one might paraphrase the verse as follows: “So in this way (through judgment) Jacob’s sin will be “atoned for,” and this is the way his sin will be removed, when he (i.e., God) makes all the altar stones like crushed limestone….” This interpretation is more consistent with the tone of judgment in vv. 8 and 10-11.
verses.commentary:
27:9 Here again many have asserted that this shows that Israel/Judah was forgiven because of the
judgment that they experienced from the hand of God. But wait, they must also destroy all remnants
of their fertility worship (lines 3, 4). However, this must be brought in line with the concept of
"the Suffering Servant" found in Isa. 52:13-53:12. Again, it is not an either/or situation, but two
different ways of looking at the actions of God in human history. The Messiah is the means of salvation,
but people must respond to Him in faith and faithfulness (note Eph. 2:8-9,10 and Phil. 2:12-13).

SPECIAL TOPIC: EASTERN LITERATURE

▣ "altar stones. . .Asherim" These were the symbols of the male and female fertility deities
of Canaan which were so devastating to the worship of YHWH. They will be destroyed!

- stones ‒ the Canaanite altars had an uplifted, uncut, oblong stone which was a phallic symbol, Exod. 23:24; Lev. 26:1; Deut. 16:22

- asherim ‒ the Canaanite symbol of the tree of life. It could be a carved piece of wood or a live tree, Exod. 34:13; Deut. 7:5; 12:3; 16:21 (a tree); Isa. 17:8

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE

SPECIAL TOPIC: ISRAEL'S MANDATED RESPONSE TO CANAANITE FERTILITY WORSHIP

▣ "chalk stones" This word (BDB 162) appears only here in the OT. It denotes a soft stone that can
easily be pulverized.

The same word is found in Dan. 5:5, but in Aramaic, and refers to the plaster on the walls of
the banquet room in the palace of Nebuchadnezzar's grandson, Belshazzar.

verses.zh: 因为坚固城变为凄凉，成了撇下离弃的居所，像旷野一样；牛犊必在那里吃草，在那里躺卧，并吃尽其中的树枝。
verses.en: For the fortified city[NOTE:1] is left alone;it is a deserted settlementand abandoned like the wilderness.Calves[NOTE:2] graze there;they lie down thereand eat its branches bare.[NOTE:3]
notes: The identity of this city is uncertain. The context suggests that an Israelite city, perhaps Samaria or Jerusalem, is in view. For discussions of interpretive options see J. N. Oswalt, Isaiah (NICOT), 1:496-97, and Paul L. Redditt, “Once Again, the City in Isaiah 24-27, ” HAR 10 (1986), 332.
The singular form in the text is probably collective.
Heb “and destroy her branches.” The city is the antecedent of the third feminine singular pronominal suffix. Apparently the city is here compared to a tree. See also v. 11.
verses.commentary:
27:10 "For the fortified city is isolated" This is another play on the term "city." See note at Isa. 24:10.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE TWO "CITIES" IN ISAIAH

verses.zh: 枝条枯干，必被折断；妇女要来点火烧着。因为这百姓蒙昧无知，所以，创造他们的必不怜恤他们；造成他们的也不施恩与他们。
verses.en: When its branches get brittle,[NOTE:1] they break;women come and use them for kindling.[NOTE:2] For these people lack understanding,[NOTE:3] therefore the one who made them has no compassion on them;the one who formed them has no mercy on them.
notes: Heb “are dry” (so NASB, NIV, NRSV).
Heb “women come [and] light it.” The city is likened to a dead tree with dried-up branches that is only good for firewood.
Heb “for not a people of understanding [is] he.”
verses.commentary:
27:11 The imagery of a deserted pasture representing the exiled, sinful people of God continues
from Isa. 27:10 in Isa. 27:11, lines 1-2.

These disobedient covenant people are characterized:

- they are not a people of discernment, cf. Hosea 4:14

- their Maker (cf. Isa. 43:1,7; 44:2,21,24; Deut. 32:18) will not have compassion on them

- their Creator will not be gracious to them

SPECIAL TOPIC: CONSEQUENCES OF IDOLATRY

verses.zh: 以色列人哪，到那日，耶和华必从大河，直到埃及小河，将你们一一地收集，如同人打树拾果一样。
verses.en: At that time[NOTE:1] the Lord will shake the tree,[NOTE:2] from the Euphrates River[NOTE:3] to the Stream of Egypt. Then you will be gathered up one by one, O Israelites.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “and it will be in that day.” The verb that introduces this verse serves as a discourse particle and is untranslated; see note on “in the future” in 2:2.

Heb “the Lord will beat out.” The verb is used of beating seeds or grain to separate the husk from the kernel (see Judg 6:11; Ruth 2:17; Isa 28:27), and of beating the olives off the olive tree (Deut 24:20). The latter metaphor may be in view here, where a tree metaphor has been employed in the preceding verses. See also 17:6.
Heb “the river,” a frequent designation in the OT for the Euphrates. For clarity most modern English versions substitute the name “Euphrates” for “the river” here.
The Israelites will be freed from exile (likened to beating the olives off the tree) and then gathered (likened to collecting the olives).
verses.commentary:
27:12-13 This seems to form a concluding literary statement. Isaiah 27:12 is talking about God's
dealings (i.e. "thresh," BDB 286, KB 285, Qal IMPERFECT which denotes
an eschatological harvest with its separation of the faithful and unfaithful, cf. Matt. 13:36-43; 24:31; 25:32).

It refers to the limits of the Promised Land found so often in the OT
(cf. Gen. 15:18; 1 Kgs. 8:65; Ezek. 47:15-19). Isaiah 27:13 is international in scope; it deals with those
Gentile nations beyond the people of God who are also invited to respond to God by faith (i.e. Isa. 2:2-4; 12:4-5;
19:18-25; 25:6-9; 42:6-12; 45:22-23; 49:5-6; 51:4-5; 56:6-7; 60:1-3; 66:23).

These last two verses reflect Deut. 30:1-10 in eschatological imagery (note Hosea 11:8-11).

It is always difficult for me to know if texts such as this refer to

- the shattered, exiled covenant people

- the OT imagery of Jerusalem as the center of YHWH's blessing and calling of all humans to Himself

My basic understanding is that Israel was a crucial element in YHWH's redemptive plan, but a
passing one (cf. book of Hebrews and the Partial Preterist interpretation of the Olivet Discourse; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: SUPERIORITY OF THE NEW COVENANT OVER THE MOSAIC COVENANT).

The NT authors' understanding of Jesus as the Jewish Messiah sent to redeem all
people changed everything. They had to reevaluate the OT prophecies about national Israel. Neither
Jesus nor any NT author ever reaffirms these national promises, but reinterprets them, universalizes them to
include all people. The NT is about Jesus, not Israel!

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

27:12 "from the flowing stream" This word (BDB 987) has two meanings.

- flowing stream, BDB 987 I, cf. Ps. 69:2,15

- gathering grain, BDB 987 II, cf. Isa. 17:5; Gen. 41:5,6,7,22,23,24,26,27; Ruth 2:2; Job 24:24

This chapter uses both senses. Number 1 fits the allusion in Isa. 27:1, but number 2 fits the
immediate VERB (thresh) and the imagery for judgment (i.e. harvesting).

▣ "the brook of Egypt" This refers to the wadi El'arish, which is the southern boundary of the
Promised Land, not the Nile River.

verses.commentary:
27:13 "in that day that a great trumpet will be blown" This is a recurrent eschatological theme using
worship or military imagery of a blown trumpet (BDB 1051).

- worship, Exod. 19:16,19; Lev. 25:9; Num. 10:2,8,10; 1 Chr. 15:24; see SPECIAL TOPIC: WORSHIP

- military, Num. 10:9; Joshua 6; Jdg. 3:27; 6:34; 7; 1 Sam. 13:3; 2 Sam. 2:28

- eschatological, here and possibly Zech. 9:14; Matt. 24:31; 1 Cor. 15:52; 1 Thess. 4:16; the seven trumpets of judgment in Rev. 8-11

- Why is Isaiah 27:6 so significant in light of God's plan for Jerusalem?

national and the international and the corporate and the individual)

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which
means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the
light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not
relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- This is the concluding chapter of the literary unit which began in Isaiah 24. These chapters are often called
"Isaiah's Apocalypse."

SPECIAL TOPIC: APOCALYPTIC LITERATURE

- The last two lines are imagery for the end-time judgment, starting with Abraham's seed
(cf. Jer. 25:29; Amos 3:2; 1 Pet. 4:17), but extending to all humans.

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

- The last verse, like Isa. 27:5, extends hope to the Gentile nations
(cf. Isa. 2:2-4; 19:18-23; 25:2-3).

- This is a wonderful poetic chapter, but its beauty causes ambiguity and confusion. Remember,
seek the meaning of strophes, not the details of poetic word plays or mythological allusions.
